notes.claim: Transposing engineering formulae is listed as a skill learners are advised to have on entry to the SQA HN Engineering Mathematics 1 unit.
Solving a linear equation and changing the subject of a formula use the same process, according to BBC Bitesize.
Oak National Academy begins its linear equations unit with the idea that the two sides of the equals sign balance.
NCETM names understanding the equals sign as meaning "having the same value as" as key to solving equations.
Some students read the equals sign as "the answer comes next" and add up the left side while ignoring the right.
Balance scales can show that the quantities on both sides of the equals sign are the same.
Balance scales have limits, and showing negative numbers on them can be challenging.
To rearrange a formula, start with the last operation and work back to the first, undoing each step with its inverse.
BBC Bitesize says solving a linear equation and changing the subject are exactly the same process, so the undoing in a flow diagram serves for both.
In one study of one-step equations, the most frequent errors were negative sign errors, followed by fractions errors.
A recorded wrong undo: a student reaches x/4 = 160 correctly, then divides instead of multiplying (called the "other inverse" error).
Balance scales have limits, and representing negative numbers on them can be challenging.
With algebra tiles, matching tiles on both sides of x + 7 = 3x + 1 can be removed, which is the same as taking the same amount off both sides.
Oak National Academy teaches that equations with unknowns on both sides can be manipulated so the unknowns end up on one side.
A formula remains balanced if the same operation is performed on both sides, which is why matching terms can come off both sides.
Ohm's law links the voltage across a resistor and the current through it, and power formulae come from combining it with the power equation.
Substituting V = IR into P = V x I gives P = I x R x I, which is I squared times R.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency General Engineering Science I maths syllabus asks candidates to form linear equations consistent with data provided.
A trade formula sheet for electricians gives power as current squared times resistance, for resistive circuits.
A teacher describes the "chuck it on the other side and it changes sign" shortcut as working for a great number of equations.
notes.contested: Bitesize National 5 teaches the shortcut "change side, change operation" as the general rule, while a teacher says it works for a great number of equations but prefers the balance method, which other Bitesize pages use.

notes.claim: BBC Bitesize National 5 (Scotland) teaches the general rule "change side, change operation" for changing the subject.
A formula remains balanced if the same operation is performed on both sides.
SQA lists the ability to transpose engineering formulae as advantageous on entry to its HN Engineering Mathematics 1 unit.
Bitesize says to start with the last operation and work back to the first.
Boyle's law relates the absolute pressure and volume of a given mass of confined gas when the temperature stays unchanged in a closed system.
Absolute pressure is the sum of gauge pressure and atmospheric pressure.
A worked cylinder example adds atmospheric pressure to the gauge pressure to get absolute pressure before using P1 x V1 = P2 x V2.
The standard atmosphere is exactly 101 325 Pa.
A cable table reproduced from BS 7671 gives voltage drop per ampere per metre, which is the unit the voltage-drop rule is built from.
Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.
Squaring both sides of an equation in general may introduce extra solutions not valid for the original equation.
Squaring and taking the square root are inverse operations, used when changing the subject of formulas with squares and roots.
